thread.title: UPDATE: More and more U.S. companies distance themselves from Saudi money due to Khashoggi affair

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: More and more U.S. companies distance themselves from Saudi money due to Khashoggi affair
text:
By Victor Reklaitis, MarketWatch
J.P. Morgan, Ford, BlackRock, Uber, New York Times, CNBC pull out of upcoming investment conference in Riyadh
As the outcry grows over the alleged murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi, possibly by Saudi Arabian agents, some U.S. companies are cutting ties with the wealthy kingdom -- and more could follow suit.
Khashoggi, a Saudi citizen and Virginia resident known for criticizing his home country's government, was allegedly killed (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/i-do-not-like-it-trump-says-of-report-saudis-killed-dismembered-journalist-2018-10-08) this month in the Middle Eastern nation's consulate in Istanbul, Turkey. The Saudi government has denied any involvement in his disappearance, including, according to President Donald Trump (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trump-sending-pompeo-to-saudi-arabia-after-king-denies-khashoggi-knowledge-2018-10-15), in a Monday phone call between Trump and Saudi King Salman.
The fallout could affect a range of U.S. companies with Saudi links, including defense contractors, banks, energy giants and media companies.
"There will be public pressure on them," said Randa Slim, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a think tank in Washington, D.C. "In the short term they might want to take some distance, but in the long term they're going to take their cues from the White House."
A growing number of companies have dropped out of Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative conference that's scheduled for next week, with J.P. Morgan Chase & Co.(JPM)CEO Jamie Dimon and Ford Motor Co.(F)Chairman Bill Ford backing out over the weekend (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/saudi-backlash-ford-chairman-latest-to-drop-out-of-riyadh-conference-but-mnuchin-still-plans-to-attend-2018-10-14). The moves to pull out from the event began last Wednesday as the New York Times Co.(NYT)said it's no longer a media sponsor of the event, also called "Davos in the Desert." Other media sponsors such as AT&T Inc.'s(T)CNN, Comcast Corp.'s(CMCSA)CNBC and the U.K.'s Financial Times also dropped out.
Uber Technologies Inc.'s Dara Khosrowshahi had been among the American CEOs slated to speak (http://futureinvestmentinitiative.com/en/article/over-100-global-business-leaders-and-innovators-confirmed-to-speak-at-fii-2018) at the Future Investment Initiative, along with J.P. Morgan's Dimon and BlackRock Inc.'s(BLK)Larry Fink, but Khosrowshahi said in a statement late Thursday that he won't take part, citing the journalist's disappearance. "I'm very troubled by the reports to date about Jamal Khashoggi. We are following the situation closely, and, unless a substantially different set of facts emerges, I won't be attending the FII conference in Riyadh," Khosrowshahi said. BlackRock's Fink also will no longer attend, according to published reports. That annual event, in its second year, is scheduled to take place Oct. 23-25 in Riyadh.
"That will be the first indicator," the Middle East Institute's Slim said last week of the conference. "If it's going to be business as usual, with only a few people pulling out, that gives you a roadmap of where this is going."
The Saudi market is "too big for businesses to lose," so there will be "pushback from the business community to limit that fallout," Slim said. She noted Congress is pushing in the other direction, as it "for a long time has had a difficult relationship with the Saudis, starting with 9/11."
The defense companies(ITA)with ties to Saudi Arabia include Raytheon Co.(RTN) , which gets 2% of its annual revenue from the country, according to FactSet data, and BAE Systems PLC (BA.LN) , a U.K.-based company with U.S. operations, which generates 17% of its sales in Saudi Arabia.
Since the columnist's disappearance, Trump has sounded skeptical about blocking arms sales to Saudi Arabia because of the Khashoggi affair. Last year, Trump signed a $110 billion arms deal (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trump-arrives-in-saudi-arabia-as-political-controversies-heat-up-at-home-2017-05-20) with the Saudis.
"I think that would be hurting us. We have jobs," the president said late last Wednesday in a Fox News interview (https://www.foxnews.com/politics/trump-talks-haley-replacement-hurricane-michael-in-exclusive-interview). He said it's "too early" to commit to "what recourse we would take." A day later, Trump played down Khashoggi's disappearance, saying (https://twitter.com/joshtpm/status/1050419885891829760) "this took place in Turkey" and "Khashoggi is not a United States citizen."
On Monday, the president said King Salman denied knowing what may have happened to Khashoggi, with Trump adding that he was "immediately" sending Secretary of State Mike Pompeo to meet with the Saudi king. While Salman is king, he named his son Mohammed bin Salman as crown prince last year, and MBS has been tightening his grip on power. The crown prince is seen as the architect (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/saudi-king-names-son-as-new-crown-prince-in-royal-shakeup-2017-06-21) of the kingdom's attempt to overhaul its oil-dependent economy and carve out a more muscular foreign policy.
"The White House modus operandi is to sweep this under the rug, or to de-escalate the situation and try to minimize the fallout in the long term," said Slim, who added that she knew Khashoggi.
Meanwhile, nearly two dozen U.S. senators signed a letter last week triggering an investigation that could result in sanctions (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/us-senators-trigger-sanctions-probe-over-missing-saudi-journalist-2018-10-10) against Saudi Arabia. Sen. Rand Paul, a Kentucky Republican, said in a tweet (https://twitter.com/RandPaul/status/1050360736919236608) on Thursday that Trump "should immediately halt arms sales and military support to Saudi Arabia." Sen. Bob Corker, a Tennessee Republican and chairman of the Senate Committee Foreign Relations, said arms sales to the country were at risk.
In other company-related developments following Khashoggi's disappearance, a Saudi futuristic megacity project announced last Tuesday that Apple Inc.(AAPL)Chief Design Officer Jony Ive was part of its advisory board, but then it revised its news release to remove Ive's name after Apple said Ive had never been part of the project, according to a BuzzFeed News report (https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/ryanmac/silicon-valley-leaders-disassociate-saudi-arabia-board-neom). Dan Doctoroff, CEO of Alphabet Inc.'s(GOOGL) (GOOGL)Sidewalk Labs, and former U.S. Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz distanced themselves from the project, called Neom, the BuzzFeed report noted. That's after they initially were announced as members of the advisory board as well.
The Khashoggi affair "could have profound implications for U.S.-Saudi relations," said Rob Malley, president and CEO of Crisis Group and a former Obama administration adviser on Mideast policy, in a tweet late Wednesday (https://twitter.com/Rob_Malley/status/1050230807544107008). "Yemen is far costlier & deadlier. But this is personal & more palpable. & media won't let go," Malley added, referring to Saudi Arabia's involvement (https://www.reuters.com/article/us-yemen-security-saudi-un/saudi-arabia-must-halt-yemen-strikes-un-child-rights-panel-idUSKCN1ML1LZ) in a civil war in Yemen.
This is an updated version of a report first published on Oct. 11, 2018.
-Victor Reklaitis;
